messages.subject: Re: run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
messages.subject_clean: run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
messages.body_plain:
Thank you, Karl.
I did the est.map for each chromosomes separately, and  c(mapchr1, mapch2,....) and then use the replace.map.
this time, for calc.geno and scanone, I use the whole dataset, but calc.genoprob give me this error message:
qtl_calcgeno_wholedataset = calc.genoprob(qtl_box21_22_c_chr1_10_SNPout_r2_0.99, step = 0.5, error.prob = 0.001)

Error in rep(0, n.gen * n.ind * n.pos) : invalid 'times' argument
In addition: Warning message:
NAs introduced by coercion

I searched the group discussions, and someone had similar error with scantwo function (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/rqtl-disc/2moKrjEWGhc),
and you mentioned:
"My guess is that the number of markers and pseudomarkers is too big for scantwo.
> x <- rep(0, 10^10)
Error in rep(0, 10^10) : invalid 'times' argument
In addition: Warning message:
NAs introduced by coercion

You might try re-running calc.genoprob with step=0 (no inserted pseudomarkers)
karl"

therefore, I tried with step = 0 in the calc.genoprob function, no error. but scanone gived the LOD score from this run is much smaller (highest = 5.72) and less than 10% of permutation LOD (n.perm = 1000, 10% of LOD = 6.75).

so if I still want use step = 1 and ger better LOD score, what should I do?
use different map.function ( Haldane, Kosambi or Carter-Falconer)? or have to cut the marker number on each chromosome (the markers are SNPs from GBS data)?

Qingming
==================================================================================================

On Monday, July 11, 2016 at 9:27:50 AM UTC-5, Qing-ming Gao wrote:

> Hi Karl,
> I have a mapping population with a large number of SNP markers, and the est.map run takes too long (so far have more than 10 days and still running, its a run on single R session).
> I am thinking to run est.map for different chromosomes in several RStudio sessions and then combine the results. Can I do this and how to combine the est.map results?
> Thanks a lot!
>
>
> Best,
> Qingming

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Re: run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
messages.body_plain:
How big is your genetic map, in cM? I wouldn't think that calc.genoprob with step = 0.5 or 1 would result in an out-of-memory problem.

Also, the LOD threshold of 6.75 is unusually large. I'd recommend looking at a histogram of the permutation results. It should be skewed, with a long right tail, but unimodal.

karl

messages.body_plain:
There's no immediate way to do this, but you might look at the code to plot.map and seek to modify it for your purposes.

  https://github.com/kbroman/qtl/blob/master/R/plot.R#L252

The function uses segments() to make the ticks at the markers. You want to add a 'col' argument to that, to use different colors for the markers with segregation distortion.

  https://github.com/kbroman/qtl/blob/master/R/plot.R#L381
  https://github.com/kbroman/qtl/blob/master/R/plot.R#L420

karl

messages.body_plain:
Those lengths look like bp rather than cM, and that's the cause of the memory problem: calc.genoprob is trying to insert a pseudomarker every bp.

First try dividing everything by 10^6, and then try estimating a genetic map.

The histogram of permutation results look okay to me, but try it again after revising the map.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic Map Construction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bryan,
Another options is to try to reduce the number of markers on a chromosome - its likely that you don't really need 493 markers, unless you have a ton of recombination.
I have a function "dropSimilarMarkers" that drops similar markers based on their recombination fraction (retaining the markers with fewer NAs and less segregation distortion).
Perhaps that would speed up your map construction.
Cheers,
John

## Find the package here: https://github.com/jtlovell/qtlTools

## To get it:
library(devtools)
install_github("jtlovell/qtlTools")
library(qtlTools)

## To run it:
?dropSimilarMarkers

## An example:
set.seed(42)
map<-sim.map(len = c(50,20), n.mar = c(20,30), include.x=F)
cross0<-sim.cross(map, n.ind=50, type="f2", map.function="kosambi", error.prob=.01, missing.prob = .05)
cross0<-est.rf(cross0)
cross1<-dropSimilarMarkers(cross0)
plot.map(cross0, cross1)

messages.body_plain:
I would suggest estimating a proper genetic map, even if it is time consuming.

But big differences in the QTL mapping results depending on the scale is really suspicious. With such high-density markers, you should essentially *know* everyone's genotype across the genome, and so the sort of "imputation" in calc.genoprob() should be immaterial.

But it's hard to tell what's going on without looking at the data.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

Thanks for the idea because I noticed some of my markers were showing segregation distortion.

On Wednesday, October 5, 2016 at 9:28:46 AM UTC-5, John Lovell wrote:

> Hi Bryan,
> Another options is to try to reduce the number of markers on a chromosome - its likely that you don't really need 493 markers, unless you have a ton of recombination.
> I have a function "dropSimilarMarkers" that drops similar markers based on their recombination fraction (retaining the markers with fewer NAs and less segregation distortion).
> Perhaps that would speed up your map construction.
> Cheers,
> John
>
> ## Find the package here: https://github.com/jtlovell/qtlTools
>
> ## To get it:
> library(devtools)
> install_github("jtlovell/qtlTools")
> library(qtlTools)
>
> ## To run it:
> ?dropSimilarMarkers
>
> ## An example:
> set.seed(42)
> map<-sim.map(len = c(50,20), n.mar = c(20,30), include.x=F)
> cross0<-sim.cross(map, n.ind=50, type="f2", map.function="kosambi", error.prob=.01, missing.prob = .05)
> cross0<-est.rf(cross0)
> cross1<-dropSimilarMarkers(cross0)
> plot.map(cross0, cross1)
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, October 4, 2016 at 12:57:39 PM UTC-5, bryan musungu wrote:
> > Thanks for the information Karl.  I was able to get it to work.  Another question I have is for the orderMarker() function takes a long time for 493 markers.  What would you suggest to speed up the analysis for orderMarker().
> >
> > On Thursday, September 29, 2016 at 10:28:06 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
> > > I wouldn't use the term "inappropriate".
> > >
> > > Small values of min.lod will result in markers being placed in the same linkage group when they're not really linked.
> > >
> > > Large values of min.lod will result in linkage groups being in multiple pieces.
> > >
> > > The values to choose depend on the type of cross, the sample size, the number of markers, and the number of chromosomes. It's hard to say in advance what to use.
> > >
> > > karl
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Sep 29, 2016, at 10:24 AM, bryan musungu <bryan....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hello Karl,

> > > > Bryan

> > > > karl

> > > >

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
messages.body_plain:
This doesn't really work. You want to adjust for the scan across the genome, and the procedure you describe would only control for the scan across a chromosome.

There's a way to use the chromosome-specific permutation results to get an overall threshold, but it would require more permutations since

Better would be to use set.seed() prior to running the permutations for each chromosome, to ensure that the permutations used are exactly the same for each chromosome, and then for each permutation replicate, maximize across the chromosomes.

But I think really you want to get the chromosomes together and do things in the traditional way. The results will be more easily obtained and more trustworthy.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic Map Construction
messages.body_plain:
For QTL mapping, we want a genetic map, in cM. Functions like calc.genoprob and sim.geno need estimated recombination fractions, which are derived from the cM locations plus a map function.

karl

> On Oct 6, 2016, at 10:47 AM, bryan musungu <bryan....@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Bryan
>
> On Tuesday, October 4, 2016 at 1:01:31 PM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
> Try using a smaller number for "window", or use use.ripple=FALSE
> Try using a lower number for maxit; say maxit=10. Likely will get a bunch of warnings about lack of convergence, but you can ignore those. When you've established marker order, go back and get improved estimates of inter-marker distances with est.map().
>
> karl
>
> > On Oct 4, 2016, at 12:57 PM, bryan musungu <bryan....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks for the information Karl.  I was able to get it to work.  Another question I have is for the orderMarker() function takes a long time for 493 markers.  What would you suggest to speed up the analysis for orderMarker().
> >
> > On Thursday, September 29, 2016 at 10:28:06 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
> > I wouldn't use the term "inappropriate".
> >
> > Small values of min.lod will result in markers being placed in the same linkage group when they're not really linked.
> >
> > Large values of min.lod will result in linkage groups being in multiple pieces.
> >
> > The values to choose depend on the type of cross, the sample size, the number of markers, and the number of chromosomes. It's hard to say in advance what to use.

> > karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
messages.body_plain:
What does the map look like when you read the data in?

Try summaryMap(mycross)

One possibility is that there are problems with the genotype data, with some markers having miscoded genotypes or in the wrong position, so that the inter-marker distances are greatly inflated.

But I can't tell from the information given.

est.map() is not going to return bp; it returns estimated cM positions using the available genotype data.

One other thing: you'd mentioned before that this is an F4 population. The estimated distances are then going to be inflated due to the multiple generations of recombination. But not inflated by *this* much.

karl

>
> There's a way to use the chromosome-specific permutation results to get an overall threshold, but it would require more permutations since
>
> Better would be to use set.seed() prior to running the permutations for each chromosome, to ensure that the permutations used are exactly the same for each chromosome, and then for each permutation replicate, maximize across the chromosomes.
>
> But I think really you want to get the chromosomes together and do things in the traditional way. The results will be more easily obtained and more trustworthy.

> karl

On Thu, Oct 6, 2016 at 3:40 PM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> What does the map look like when you read the data in?
>
> Try summaryMap(mycross)
>
> One possibility is that there are problems with the genotype data, with some markers having miscoded genotypes or in the wrong position, so that the inter-marker distances are greatly inflated.
>
> But I can't tell from the information given.
>
> est.map() is not going to return bp; it returns estimated cM positions using the available genotype data.
>
> One other thing: you'd mentioned before that this is an F4 population. The estimated distances are then going to be inflated due to the multiple generations of recombination. But not inflated by *this* much.
>
> karl
>
>

> >             n.mar    length ave.spacing max.spacing
> > 10        39404   4340518       110.2      1001.5
> > overall 39404   4340518       110.2      1001.5
> >
> > seems like its take bp not cM during the run of est.map, why like this? (I set estimate.map = true when I read.cross(mycross), is this the reason? )
> >
> > Thanks!

> > On Thu, Oct 6, 2016 at 1:30 PM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > This doesn't really work. You want to adjust for the scan across the genome, and the procedure you describe would only control for the scan across a chromosome.
> >
> > There's a way to use the chromosome-specific permutation results to get an overall threshold, but it would require more permutations since
> >
> > Better would be to use set.seed() prior to running the permutations for each chromosome, to ensure that the permutations used are exactly the same for each chromosome, and then for each permutation replicate, maximize across the chromosomes.
> >
> > But I think really you want to get the chromosomes together and do things in the traditional way. The results will be more easily obtained and more trustworthy.
> >
> > karl
> >
> > > On Oct 5, 2016, at 11:36 AM, Gao, Qing-ming <qingmi...@uky.edu> wrote:

> > > I am thinking to do 17 X 1000 times (equal to 1000 times whole genome permutation), and concatenate the 17 x 1000 permutations, pick top 1% [ (950 + 16*1000)/17000 ] from this 17000, which is equal to 5% of each chromosome permutation each 1000 permutation (950/1000).
> > > does this calculation make sense?
> > >
> > >
> > > Qingming
> > >
> > > On Wed, Oct 5, 2016 at 10:25 AM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I would suggest estimating a proper genetic map, even if it is time consuming.
> > >
> > > But big differences in the QTL mapping results depending on the scale is really suspicious. With such high-density markers, you should essentially *know* everyone's genotype across the genome, and so the sort of "imputation" in calc.genoprob() should be immaterial.
> > >
> > > But it's hard to tell what's going on without looking at the data.
> > >
> > > karl

On Thu, Oct 6, 2016 at 3:40 PM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> What does the map look like when you read the data in?
>
> Try summaryMap(mycross)
>
> One possibility is that there are problems with the genotype data, with some markers having miscoded genotypes or in the wrong position, so that the inter-marker distances are greatly inflated.
>
> But I can't tell from the information given.
>
> est.map() is not going to return bp; it returns estimated cM positions using the available genotype data.
>
> One other thing: you'd mentioned before that this is an F4 population. The estimated distances are then going to be inflated due to the multiple generations of recombination. But not inflated by *this* much.
>
> karl
>
>

> > first row marker name, second row chr name, third row is the marker position (Mbp/10^6, actually its physical location on chromosome) .
> >

> >             n.mar    length ave.spacing max.spacing
> > 10        39404   4340518       110.2      1001.5
> > overall 39404   4340518       110.2      1001.5
> >
> > seems like its take bp not cM during the run of est.map, why like this? (I set estimate.map = true when I read.cross(mycross), is this the reason? )
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> >
> > On Thu, Oct 6, 2016 at 1:30 PM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > This doesn't really work. You want to adjust for the scan across the genome, and the procedure you describe would only control for the scan across a chromosome.
> >
> > There's a way to use the chromosome-specific permutation results to get an overall threshold, but it would require more permutations since
> >
> > Better would be to use set.seed() prior to running the permutations for each chromosome, to ensure that the permutations used are exactly the same for each chromosome, and then for each permutation replicate, maximize across the chromosomes.
> >
> > But I think really you want to get the chromosomes together and do things in the traditional way. The results will be more easily obtained and more trustworthy.
> >
> > karl
> >
> > > On Oct 5, 2016, at 11:36 AM, Gao, Qing-ming <qingmi...@uky.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > Thank you, Karl.
> > > I will make a new genetic map then.
> > >
> > >
> > > While I am waiting for the new map, I am thinking to use the old map data without rescale, cause I already finished calc.genoprob() and scanone() based on each chromosome. the next is doing the permutation on each chromosome (sorry, I have asked you this question before).
> > > I am thinking to do 17 X 1000 times (equal to 1000 times whole genome permutation), and concatenate the 17 x 1000 permutations, pick top 1% [ (950 + 16*1000)/17000 ] from this 17000, which is equal to 5% of each chromosome permutation each 1000 permutation (950/1000).
> > > does this calculation make sense?
> > >
> > >
> > > Qingming
> > >
> > > On Wed, Oct 5, 2016 at 10:25 AM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I would suggest estimating a proper genetic map, even if it is time consuming.
> > >
> > > But big differences in the QTL mapping results depending on the scale is really suspicious. With such high-density markers, you should essentially *know* everyone's genotype across the genome, and so the sort of "imputation" in calc.genoprob() should be immaterial.
> > >
> > > But it's hard to tell what's going on without looking at the data.
> > >
> > > karl
> > >
> > >

messages.subject: addqtl: what is strong evidence for additional qtl
messages.subject_clean: addqtl: what is strong evidence for additional qtl
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

I have a follow-up question after my previous post about error when running stepwiseqtl. As I am working on 4-way cross, which stepwiseqtl doesn't aim at. So I guess the only way to employ MQM is to use makeqtl and addqtl.

The procedure I followed is that I make a preliminary multiple QTL model using makeqtl based on the result of scanone and scantwo and then refine the model using refineqtl. The next step is to estimate the effect of all QLTs and interactions by fitqtl including a drop-one test. Then I check for additional qtl by running addqtl. If I find some qtls with very high LOD score, then I go back to makeqtl and revise the formula by adding those QTL with high LOD. Those procedures are implemented iteratively unless no more additional qtls found by addqtl. Then the final model is refined by refineqtl and its effect is estimated. Do such procedures make sense?

However, I am not sure how to determine the threshold of LOD score when searching additional qtl with "addqtl". The other information I can use is to check the phenotypic traits accross genotypes at potential QTL with relatively high LOD found by "addqtl". Do you have any suggestions on determining LOD threshold or other threshold for clear evidence of additional qtls?

Thank you a lot!

Best wishes,
Xiaodong

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] CIM results
messages.body_plain:
The LOD scores are provided directly in the output of cim().

To get a likelihood ratio statistic, multiply the LOD scores by 2*log(10).

To get a significance threshold, perform a permutation test by running cim() with the n.perm argument specified.

We don't have a way to get effect estimates or phenotypic variance explained except through the fitqtl() function. Once you've decided on some set of QTL, use makeqtl() to create a "qtl object" and then fitqtl() with get.ests=TRUE to get estimated effects and estimated percent variance explained.

karl

>
> The procedure I followed is that I make a preliminary multiple QTL model using makeqtl based on the result of scanone and scantwo and then refine the model using refineqtl. The next step is to estimate the effect of all QLTs and interactions by fitqtl including a drop-one test. Then I check for additional qtl by running addqtl. If I find some qtls with very high LOD score, then I go back to makeqtl and revise the formula by adding those QTL with high LOD. Those procedures are implemented iteratively unless no more additional qtls found by addqtl. Then the final model is refined by refineqtl and its effect is estimated. Do such procedures make sense?
>

That's basically what stepwiseqtl() does.

> However, I am not sure how to determine the threshold of LOD score when searching additional qtl with "addqtl". The other information I can use is to check the phenotypic traits accross genotypes at potential QTL with relatively high LOD found by "addqtl". Do you have any suggestions on determining LOD threshold or other threshold for clear evidence of additional qtls?

I use a penalized LOD score, penalizing each QTL by the significance threshold obtained from a permutation test with a single-QTL scan. See the chapter 9 of the R/qtl book, http://rqtl.org/book

I hope to fix stepwiseqtl() and related functions to work properly for four-way cross data, but I've not had time to work on it yet.

> The LOD scores are provided directly in the output of cim().
>
> To get a likelihood ratio statistic, multiply the LOD scores by 2*log(10).
>
> To get a significance threshold, perform a permutation test by running cim() with the n.perm argument specified.
>
> We don't have a way to get effect estimates or phenotypic variance explained except through the fitqtl() function. Once you've decided on some set of QTL, use makeqtl() to create a "qtl object" and then fitqtl() with get.ests=TRUE to get estimated effects and estimated percent variance explained.

The 5% significance threshold from your permutation results is ~3.89, higher than the maximum LOD score from your scanone results. That's why the stepwiseqtl results indicate no QTL.

The scanone summary will show marker names, and so I would understand "S1_3689817~S1_3875425~S1_4247522" to be the name of a single marker column in your genotype data.

karl

messages.body_plain:
>From the results you present and the permutation results you got, it doesn't look like there's any very strong evidence for interactions.

So maybe focus on the two suggestive QTL from the single-QTL scan.

Generally I'd suggest saying what you did and what you found: the single-QTL analysis indicated weak evidence for a couple of loci. The two-dimensional scan and multiple-QTL analyses didn't provide any evidence for further loci, or for interactions among loci.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This is a bit off-topic but I thought I asked anyway.
What would be the best way to plot a given trait from multiple lines (> 50) across time? I normally use a color of the parents and another for the RILs but the plot is still messy.
Any thoughts?
Thanks
L

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Multi variables plots
messages.body_plain:
It depends on what you're trying to show. One approach is to use light gray for the individual lines, and then the parents with darker colors. Another would be to use a heat map.

When you get beyond ~20 curves, plotting the individual curves becomes a mess.

Maybe take a look at Figures 3 and 4 in this paper: https://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman/publications/gough.pdf

karl

messages.body_plain:
I would study the estimated map to figure out what's going wrong. Is it a small number of markers that seem to be misplaced, or is the entire map inflated?

If all marker intervals are large, I would look at whether you've coded the genotypes correctly.

karl

messages.subject: qtlTools - an R package for plotting and exploration of R/qtl results
messages.subject_clean: qtlTools - an R package for plotting and exploration of R/qtl results
messages.body_plain:
Hi R/qtl users,
I wanted to bring your attention to an R package I am developing that adds some plotting and other functionality to R/qtl - "qtlTools".
qtlTools contains a number of functions, including methods to:
Plot QTL confidence intervals on a genetic map
Extract statistics from multiple QTL models
Compile confidence intervals from either scanone, or multiple qtl models
Strategies to reduce the number of markers in large genotype matrices
GWERk permutations
The package can be found here: https://github.com/jtlovell/qtlTools

You can install it using the following commands:
> library(devtools)
> install_github("jtlovell/qtlTools")
> library(qtlTools)

There are a number of tutorials included with the package. These, and other information can be found here: http://lovelleeb.weebly.com/qtltools

Please reply to this post if you have questions, find bugs, or have ideas for additional functionality.
Cheers, John

John T. Lovell
University of Texas at Austin

Fig. 8 in your great introduction to genetic map construction provides an extremely useful way of determining contig order to generate larger scaffolds. Thanks, David

messages.subject_clean: est.rf with one marker against all
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,
Your approach sounds really interesting.

You've run into a standard problem - 25k x 25k matrices are too large to estimate in R. I find, 10k x 10k is about as big as I can go.
Why not try to cull your matrix? You definitely won't need 25k markers in your final map ... more likely 5k at most.

You could apply qtlTools::dropSimilarMarkers (http://lovelleeb.weebly.com/qtltools) to each chromosome (assuming each chr is <10k markers).
You could then push the resultant smaller genotype matrix through your pipeline.
John

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm doing qtl analysis in a tomato riself population (ca. 3000 markers, 130 individuals). My sacnone plot for several traits suggest more than one qtl per chromosome in one or more chromosomes. See attached example for all chromosomes and zoom-in on chr 11. I'm trying to get summary of all peaks (that will include position and support interval), but scanone summaries take only the most significant qtl at a given chromosome.

So, my question is: Is there a way to get this data, rather than manually look at the output lods and plots?

In this specific example, while for chr 2 and 3, model-selection (using makeqtl, addqtl, fitqtl, refineqtl and swqtl) did a great job refining qtl position, it indicates only one qtl for chr 11. These three qtl on chr 11 are supported also from earlier works by others so I'm quite confidence about them.

Thanks,

Itay

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic Map Construction
messages.body_plain:
The run time for calc.errorlod increases with both number of markers and number of individuals.
I think it's linear in individuals and quadratic in the number of markers.

If you use calc.errorlod with version="old", it uses a somewhat different approach that is a lot faster and with computation time increasing linearly in the number of markers. But the newer (slower) version does a better job of picking out potential errors.

Personally, I no longer much use calc.errorlod; I instead rely on the HMM functions like calc.genoprob to smooth over genotyping errors without trying to pick out and clean the individual errors.

karl

messages.subject: Identifying duplicate individuals
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

I followed the tutorial for genetic map construction to check if there were any individuals in my population with over 90% matching genotypes.  These pairs were identified as follows:

      row col
 [1,]  30  31
 [2,]  41  42
 [3,]  30  55
 [4,]  31  55
 [5,]  67  69
 [6,]  54  75
 [7,]  15  79
 [8,]  80  82
 [9,]  27  85

Next, I used a piece of code that I saw you suggest to another poster (since my organism has 20 chromosomes).  This removes 8 individuals from the analysis.  And the code I'm talking about is this:

for(j in chrnames(mapthis)) {
    g <- pull.geno(mapthis, chr=j)
    for(i in 1:nrow(wh)) {
        tozero <- !is.na <http://is.na/>(g[wh[i,1],]) & !is.na <http://is.na/>(g[wh[i,2],]) & g[wh[i,1],] != g[wh[i,2],]
        mapthis$geno[[j]]$data[wh[i,1], tozero] <- NA
    }
}

Now, my question:  I have not finished phenotyping all of my individuals.  Should I skip phenotyping the individuals that I know will get deleted due to them having more than 90% similar genomes?  If I wanted to do this, how would I identify which individuals these are?

The first "phenotype" column in my dataset is not a phenotype, but rather the number assigned to each individual.  For the pairs identified in the first part, does this refer to the individuals' order in my dataset?  Ie, for the pair (30, 31), does this correspond to the 30th and 31st rows in my dataset?

Hope this makes sense.

Thanks,

Vanessa

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: F1 CP population
messages.body_plain:
The question is related to the Onemap program, I hope someone here may able to help me.

I have two crosses with 350 F1 CP progenies each, since I genotyped these populations using GBS, the parental data is missing for some SNPs. My question is how to code those progenies to the Onemap format where the parental pattern is missing.

For example:

Case 1 (one parent is missing):

Female parent: AA | Male parent (missing): 00

Progenies: AA, TT, AT, TT ………

Case 2 (both the parents are missing):

Female parent(missing): 00 | Male parent (missing): 00

Progenies: GG, GA, AA………

How to code these progenies, since I don’t know parental patterns? I appreciate any sort of help.

Thanks

Ramesh

> Now, my question:  I have not finished phenotyping all of my individuals.  Should I skip phenotyping the individuals that I know will get deleted due to them having more than 90% similar genomes?  If I wanted to do this, how would I identify which individuals these are?

It depends on cost, and whether you'll have an opportunity to re-derive DNA and re-genotype the problem samples.

>

Yes, those numbers are rows in the data. If you could include a phenotype column named "id", such identifiers will be shown instead.

karl
